title: Standard Chartered Expands Quantum Computing Research Program Following Successful Research Phase
excerpt: Standard Chartered is expanding its quantum computing research program after a first year supported by the Monetary Authority of Singapore.
content:
Insider Brief

  • Standard Chartered is expanding its quantum computing research program after a first year supported by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, with work spanning language modeling, forecasting and derivatives pricing.
  • In tests, a quantum-inspired method for adapting language models used about one-eighteenth as many trainable parameters as conventional methods, while a hybrid forecasting approach improved predictions with 28% fewer parameters.
  • Quantum algorithms matched conventional derivatives pricing accuracy in tests using as little as one-eighteenth the number of iterations.

PRESS RELEASE — Standard Chartered today announced the expansion of its quantum computing research programme, following the successful completion of its first year of research supported under the Financial Sector Technology & Innovation (FSTI) Quantum Technology scheme, administered by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS)1. The expansion reinforces the Bank’s commitment to exploring emerging technologies that could transform financial services. 

In its first year, the programme explored quantum and quantum-inspired approaches for language modelling, time-series forecasting – the analysis of sequentially ordered, time-stamped data, and the pricing of financial derivatives. 

Large language models are computationally expensive to train and deploy, while quantum language models remain at an early stage of development. Quantum specialists at Standard Chartered used knowledge distillation to help a smaller quantum language model learn from a larger classical model, aiming to narrow the performance gap and explore more resource-efficient approaches to language processing. 

Quantum-inspired adapters for fine-tuning, lightweight components that enable large language models to be efficiently adapted to specialist tasks such as credit risk assessment, were also explored. Across the evaluated scenarios, the approach demonstrated strong and consistent performance while reducing the number of trainable parameters by a factor of 18 compared with classical baseline methods reported in literature.

The programme also examined the challenge of forecasting in volatile markets and changing economic conditions. In the evaluated research scenarios, combining conventional forecasting models with quantum techniques improved predictive performance while using 28% fewer parameters.

The final workstream explored the pricing of complex financial derivatives, a computationally demanding task that plays an important role in risk management and investment strategies. In the scenarios evaluated, quantum algorithms achieved comparable pricing accuracy with up to 18 times fewer computational iterations, highlighting the potential of quantum-enhanced methods to improve the efficiency of financial modelling. 

Standard Chartered is collaborating with OQC, Quantinuum, Rigetti and Qubitra, organisations that share the Bank’s commitment to advancing practical quantum research and exploring the future application of quantum computing in financial services. The programme provides access to a range of quantum computing hardware, software, simulation tools and research capabilities, enabling the Bank to deepen its research across a targeted set of use cases relevant to financial services.  

The programme focuses on understanding the specific classes of problems where quantum techniques may add value alongside classical approaches, while building the expertise, partnerships and capabilities needed for future adoption. 

Elena Strbac, Global Head, Data Science & Innovation, Corporate & Investment Bank at Standard Chartered, said: “The biggest risk with quantum is waiting for certainty before getting started. By the time the technology matures, the organisations best placed to benefit will be those that have already learned where it adds value, where it doesn’t, and what it takes to use it well. Quantum is not a universal solution. Our approach is deliberately selective, focusing our experimentation on the problems where the potential for quantum to outperform classical approaches is greatest.” 

The next phase of the programme will build on the findings from the first year, while continuing to assess the readiness of quantum technologies for adoption within highly regulated financial services environments.
